items.title: Contributing
items.text:
We welcome:

  1. Additional data type converters
  2. Validation enhancements and edge-case handling
  3. Improved documentation examples / tutorials
  4. Bug reports with minimal reproduction scripts

Workflow (after forking or a feature branch):

uv sync --group dev
uv run pytest -q
uv run ruff check .
uv sync --group docs
uv run pdoc confkit -o docs/api
uv run zensical build --clean

Before opening a PR, ensure:

  • All tests pass (including property-based tests)
  • No ruff or type errors (pyright config in project)
  • Updated docs where behavior changed

items.title: Supported Python Versions
items.text:
confkit follows the Python version support policy as outlined in the Python Developer's Guide:

  • We support all active and maintenance releases of Python above 3.11
  • End-of-life (EOL) Python versions are not supported
  • We aim to support Python release candidates to stay ahead of the release cycle

This ensures that confkit remains compatible with current Python versions while allowing us to leverage modern language features.

items.title: When to Use confkit
items.text:
Use confkit when you want:

  • Simple, configuration management
  • Type conversion and validation baked in
  • Declarative, descriptor-based definitions instead of manual parsing

If you need hierarchical, nested config trees or schema evolution with migrations, pair confkit with a higher-level orchestrator or consider extending with custom data types.

items.title: CI workflows
items.text: Every check runs from one workflow, .github/workflows/ci.yml. Its first job, changes, compares the push or PR against .github/ci-filters.yml. Each check only starts when one of its inputs changed, so a docs-only PR doesn't run the tests.

items.title: Workflow files
items.text:
File What it does Runs when these change ci.yml Decides which checks run, then calls them in order. Every push and PR to master test.yml Runs pytest on Python 3.11 to 3.14, and imports the built wheel with only its declared dependencies. src/, tests/, pyproject.toml, uv.lock lint.yml (lint) Runs ruff, ty and undersort on the package. src/, tests/, examples/, ruff.toml, pyproject.toml, uv.lock lint.yml (lint-public) Runs ruff, ty, pyrefly, zuban, mypy and pyright on examples/, the way users call the public API. src/, examples/, ruff.toml, pyproject.toml, uv.lock gitleaks.yml Scans the history for leaked secrets. Every push and PR docs.yml Builds this site, publishes PR previews and deploys master. src/, docs/, zensical.toml, mkdocs.yml, pyproject.toml, uv.lock coverage.yml Uploads coverage to Coveralls. It's informational, so nothing waits on it. src/, tests/, examples/, pyproject.toml, uv.lock bump-version-by-labels.yml Opens a version bump PR from the merged PR's Major, Minor or Patch label. Pushes to master release.yml Tags and releases a version that has no tag yet, then triggers pypi.yml. Pushes to master pypi.yml Builds the package and publishes it to PyPI. A release from release.yml

A change to ci.yml, ci-filters.yml or .github/actions/setup/ reruns every check.

Test, lint, coverage and the docs build also cache their result. The cache key hashes the check's inputs, uv.lock and its workflow files. On a hit, the check skips its heavy steps, because these exact inputs already passed. The lint dependency group pins every lint tool, so a tool upgrade changes uv.lock and the key.

items.title: When a PR is opened or updated
items.text:
flowchart TD
    open([PR opened, updated or reopened]) --> changes[changes: compare against ci-filters.yml]
    open --> gitleaks[gitleaks]
    changes -->|test inputs changed| test[test: pytest 3.11 to 3.14, clean install]
    changes -->|lint inputs changed| lint[lint: ruff, ty, undersort]
    changes -->|lint-public inputs changed| lintpub[lint-public: six type checkers on examples]
    changes -->|docs inputs changed| build[docs build]
    build -->|PR from this repo| preview[preview: publish to gh-pages/pr-previews/pr-n and comment the link]
    test --> all[all-checks]
    lint --> all
    lintpub --> all
    gitleaks --> all
    build --> all
    all --> result([PR shows pass or fail])

A check whose inputs didn't change is skipped, and all-checks counts a skipped check as passed. all-checks fails only when a check failed or was cancelled, which makes it the one check to require in branch protection.

A newer push to the same PR cancels the older run. PRs from forks build the docs but get no preview, because their token can't push to gh-pages.

items.title: When a PR is closed
items.text:
flowchart TD
    closed([PR closed or merged]) --> remove[docs remove-preview: delete gh-pages/pr-previews/pr-n]

No checks run on close. A merged PR also starts the push flow below.

items.title: When a PR is merged to master
items.text:
flowchart TD
    push([Push to master]) --> changes[changes: compare against ci-filters.yml]
    push --> gitleaks[gitleaks]
    changes -->|test inputs changed| test[test]
    changes -->|lint inputs changed| lint[lint]
    changes -->|lint-public inputs changed| lintpub[lint-public]
    changes -->|docs inputs changed| build[docs build]
    changes -->|coverage inputs changed| coverage[coverage: upload to Coveralls]
    build --> deploy[docs deploy: publish to the gh-pages root, keeping pr-previews]
    test --> all[all-checks]
    lint --> all
    lintpub --> all
    gitleaks --> all
    build --> all
    all -->|passed| bump[bump: read the merged PR's label]
    bump -->|Major, Minor or Patch| bumppr[open a bump PR]
    bump --> release[release: is the version in pyproject.toml tagged?]
    release -->|no tag yet| tag[create the tag and GitHub release]
    tag --> pypi[pypi.yml: build and publish to PyPI]
    release -->|already tagged| done([done])

The release job also creates a Sentry release on every run, whether or not the version is new.

Coverage runs next to the checks but isn't part of the chain, so a Coveralls problem never blocks a release.

Each push to master gets its own run, so a quick series of merges can't cancel a run and lose its version bump.

items.title: How a release happens
items.text:
A release takes two merges.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as You
    participant CI as ci.yml on master
    participant Bump as bump PR
    Dev->>CI: merge a PR labelled Minor
    CI->>Bump: all-checks passed, open "bump version to 2.3.0"
    CI->>CI: release finds 2.2.0 already tagged and stops
    Dev->>CI: merge the bump PR
    CI->>CI: the bump PR has no label, so bump does nothing
    CI->>CI: release finds 2.3.0 untagged, tags it and publishes to PyPI

The first merge only opens the bump PR, because the version on master hasn't changed yet. Merging the bump PR changes pyproject.toml, and the run for that push releases it.

items.title: Usage
items.text: This page explains how to work with confkit and how the documentation is generated.

items.title: Descriptor Quickstart
items.text:
from pathlib import Path
from confkit import Config

# 1. Configure confkit file (parser is auto-detected)
Config.set_file(Path("config.ini"))

# 2. Define your (class)variables with their default values
class AppConfig:
    debug = Config(False)
    port = Config(8080)

# 3. use them!
# (this value came from the .ini file!) 
print(AppConfig.port)

items.title: Adding a New Data Type
items.text:
1. Subclass BaseDataType[T]
  2. Implement convert(self, value: str) -> T
  3. (Optional) override __str__ for serialization
  4. Use via Config(CustomType(default_value))
from pathlib import Path
from confkit import Config
from confkit.data_types import BaseDataType

# 1. Configure confkit file (parser is auto-detected)
Config.set_file(Path("config.ini"))

# 2. Define the custom converter, with a convert method (from str -> your_type)
class UpperString(BaseDataType[str]):
    def convert(self, value: str) -> str:  # str from configuration -> normalized value
        return str(value).upper()

    def __str__(self, value: str):  # value -> string for configuration
        return value.upper()

# 3. Use the custom datatype inside a config class
class CustomCfg:
    shout_name = Config(UpperString("confkit"))

print(CustomCfg.shout_name)  # -> CONFKIT
CustomCfg.shout_name = "mixedCase"
print(CustomCfg.shout_name)  # -> MIXEDCASE

Full runnable example: examples/custom_data_type.py.

items.title: Optional Values
items.text:
Either pass optional=True to Config(...) or wrap a data type in Optional(...).

from confkit.data_types import Optional, String

class Service:
    api_key = Config("", optional=True)                    # primitive optional
    token = Config(Optional(String("")))                   # wrapped optional

items.title: Decorators Overview
items.text:
• Config.set(section, option, value) – always sets before call
  • Config.default(section, option, value) – sets only when missing
  • Config.with_setting(descriptor) – injects descriptor value by name
  • Config.with_kwarg(section, option, name?, default?) – inject by strings

See also: the dedicated reference pages for cross-linked signatures.

items.title: Regenerating API Docs (pdoc + zensical)
items.text:
The site is built with zensical, which reads the mkdocs.yml config and uses the mkdocstrings and pdoc plugins for deep API symbol cross-references. The api/ directory inside docs/ is produced by pdoc. Regenerate it after changing code-level docstrings or adding new public classes/functions.

uv run pdoc confkit -o docs/api --force

Key points:

  1. --force overwrites existing output
  2. The pdoc plugin (configured in mkdocs.yml as pdoc: { api_path: api }) enables links like (pdoc:confkit.config.Config) inside Markdown
  3. Reference pages in reference/ intentionally use those links for stable deep-links

items.title: Examples Overview
items.text:
This section provides runnable examples demonstrating how to use confkit in different scenarios. Each example page includes:

  • Purpose & concepts demonstrated
  • Required setup (if any)
  • How to run the example
  • Expected / generated .ini configuration contents
  • Notes & variations you can try

items.title: Quick Start: Running Examples
items.text:
All examples assume you are in the project root and have dependencies installed (only the library itself is needed for runtime examples):

uv run python examples/basic.py

If you are editing examples and want immediate persistence, remember that Config.write_on_edit defaults to True unless explicitly disabled.

Select an example in the navigation to dive in.

items.title: Purpose
items.text: Shows how to combine CLI argument parsing with confkit-backed defaults while keeping runtime-provided values separate from persisted configuration.

items.title: Key Concepts
items.text:
• Use descriptors to define defaults (AppConfig)
  • Reuse those defaults when defining CLI args
  • Disable write-on-edit (Config.write_on_edit = False) to avoid persisting transient CLI overrides
  • Maintain a clean separation between runtime arguments and persistent config

items.title: Running
items.text: uv run python examples/argparse_example.py --host 0.0.0.0 --port 9090 --debug --tags alpha beta

items.title: Generated Files
items.text:
Only config.ini is used for the descriptors; CLI values are not written because write_on_edit is disabled.

Example baseline (first run):

[AppConfig]
debug = False
host = 127.0.0.1
port = 8000
tags = example,demo

After running with overrides, the file remains unchanged (transient values do not persist):

[AppConfig]
debug = False
host = 127.0.0.1
port = 8000
tags = example,demo

items.title: Notes
items.text:
• If you enable Config.write_on_edit = True, assignments to descriptors (not argparse inputs) will persist.
  • You can sync back only selected CLI values by explicitly assigning them to descriptors after parsing.

items.title: Try Variations
items.text:
• Manually edit config.ini default port and re-run with a different CLI value.
  • Set write_on_edit = True temporarily and manually assign AppConfig.port = args.port after parsing.

items.title: Purpose
items.text:
Demonstrates the foundational usage of confkit:

  • Setting a parser + backing file
  • Defining a config class with different primitive types
  • Automatic persistence via Config.write_on_edit
  • Accessing & mutating values via descriptor access

items.title: Code Summary
items.text: examples/basic.py defines AppConfig with boolean, int, string, float, and optional string fields.

items.title: Running
items.text:
uv run python examples/basic.py

If config.ini does not yet exist it will be created automatically.

items.title: Generated / Updated config.ini
items.text:
A first run typically produces something like:

[AppConfig]
debug = False
port = 8080
host = localhost
timeout = 30.5
api_key =

After the script executes (it changes port and sets api_key), the file becomes:

[AppConfig]
debug = False
port = 9000
host = localhost
timeout = 30.5
api_key = my-secret-key

items.title: Try Variations
items.text:
• Set Config.write_on_edit = False and observe that changes are not written.
  • Manually edit config.ini then re-run to see those values picked up.

items.title: Key Takeaways
items.text: The descriptor interface gives you type-safe access. Mutations immediately persist (when enabled) without needing manual write calls.

items.title: Purpose
items.text:
Shows how to create and use a custom BaseDataType implementation.

  • Normalize and persist a value in a consistent representation
  • Demonstrate the required convert method
  • (Optionally) override __str__ for serialization formatting

items.title: Implementation
items.text:
from pathlib import Path
from confkit import Config
from confkit.data_types import BaseDataType

# Configure config file (parser is automatically detected from extension)
Config.set_file(Path("config.ini"))

class UpperString(BaseDataType[str]):
    """String that is always stored / returned in UPPER CASE."""
    def convert(self, value: str) -> str:  # raw configuration -> normalized
        return str(value).upper()

    def __str__(self, value: str):  # normalized -> persisted string
        return value.upper()

class CustomCfg:
    shout_name = Config(UpperString("confkit"))

print(CustomCfg.shout_name)  # CONFKIT
CustomCfg.shout_name = "MixedCase"
print(CustomCfg.shout_name)  # MIXEDCASE

items.title: Generated File Snippet
items.text:
After the first run (values normalized):

[CustomCfg]
shout_name = CONFKIT

After reassignment:

[CustomCfg]
shout_name = MIXEDCASE

items.title: Design Notes
items.text:
• convert should raise an appropriate exception (let BaseDataType.validate help if you call it) when input cannot be parsed.
  • Override validate if you need domain rules (e.g. length limits). Call super().validate() if stacking behavior.
  • __str__ mainly matters when you want the persisted form to differ from str(value).

items.title: Integration Checklist
items.text:
1. Create subclass class X(BaseDataType[T]):
  2. Implement convert(self, value: str) -> T
  3. (Optional) override __str__(self, value: T) -> str
  4. (Optional) override validate(self, value: T) for domain constraints.
  5. Use with Config(X(default_value))

  • Source example: examples/custom_data_type.py

items.title: Purpose
items.text:
Showcases the breadth of built-in and helper data types:

  • Explicit vs implicit (auto-detected) types
  • Numeric formatting (Hex, Octal, Binary)
  • Custom base integers (encoded as <base>c<value> in the file)
  • Bytes → integer conversion via Binary

items.title: Running
items.text: uv run python examples/data_types.py

items.title: Generated config.ini (Excerpt)
items.text:
Values may accumulate across runs; representative first-run section:

[DataTypeConfig]
string_value = default string
int_value = 42
float_value = 3.14159
bool_value = True
auto_string = auto-detected string
auto_int = 100
auto_float = 2.71828
auto_bool = False
hex_value = 0xff
octal_value = 0o755
binary_value = 0b10101010
binary_from_bytes = 0b0110100001100101011011000110110001101111
base7_value = 7c42
base5_value = 5c13

After updates inside the script, the file reflects the new values (hex, octal, binary adjustments).

items.title: Notes
items.text:
• Changing base persists a prefixed representation so it can be reliably parsed later.
  • Binary will store integers; when constructed from bytes, those bytes are interpreted as a big-endian integer.
  • Hex normalizes values by dropping leading zeros (e.g. 0x000f becomes 0xf).

items.title: Try Variations
items.text:
• Manually edit hex_value to 0x1a2b and re-run.
  • Remove binary_from_bytes line; script re-creates it.

items.title: Custom Type Extension
items.text: See the separate custom data type example examples/custom_data_type.py for how to implement and register your own converter (e.g. an UpperString normalizer) by subclassing BaseDataType.

items.title: Purpose
items.text:
Shows how to inject configuration values into functions using decorators:

  • @Config.with_setting(descriptor) — injects kwarg named after descriptor
  • @Config.with_kwarg(section, option, kwarg_name, default) — inject by strings + custom kwarg name

items.title: Running
items.text: uv run python examples/decorators.py

items.title: Behavior
items.text: ServiceConfig.retry_count and ServiceConfig.timeout are standard descriptors. The decorators wrap the functions so when called, kwargs contain the current config values.

items.title: Example Output (first run)
items.text: Processing with 3 retries

items.title: Notes
items.text:
• The with_kwarg variant does not require direct descriptor reference (less type-safe, more flexible).
  • You can still override the injected kwarg manually when calling the function; manual kwargs win.

items.title: Try Variations
items.text: • Replace with_kwarg with with_setting referencing a different descriptor.

items.title: Purpose
items.text: Shows how one setting can read and write a setting in another config file, so that file holds the only copy of the value.

items.title: Key Concepts
items.text:
• Delegate(Settings.dashboard_url) passes reads and writes through to Settings.dashboard_url
  • The delegate stores nothing, so its own file gets no key for it
  • Type checkers see the delegate with the target's type

items.title: Running
items.text: uv run python examples/delegate.py

items.title: Code
items.text:
The bot and the dashboard both read app.ini. Only the dashboard reads dashboard.ini. The dashboard's public address lives in app.ini, and dashboard.ini refers to it:

from pathlib import Path
from typing import TypeVar

from confkit.config import Config
from confkit.ext.delegate import Delegate

T = TypeVar("T")
class AppConfig(Config[T]): ...
class DashboardConfig(Config[T]): ...

AppConfig.set_file(Path("app.ini"))
DashboardConfig.set_file(Path("dashboard.ini"))

class Settings:
    dashboard_url = AppConfig("http://localhost:8001")

class DashboardSettings:
    session_key = DashboardConfig("change-me")
    public_url = Delegate(Settings.dashboard_url)

items.title: Generated Files
items.text:
app.ini holds the value:

[Settings]
dashboard_url = http://localhost:8001

dashboard.ini has no public_url key:

[DashboardSettings]
session_key = change-me

items.title: Notes
items.text:
• Reading DashboardSettings.public_url reads the dashboard_url key in app.ini.
  • DashboardSettings().public_url = "https://dashboard.example.com" writes the dashboard_url key in app.ini.
  • A delegate can point at another delegate. Both read and write the same key.
  • Pass a plain attribute read of a Config setting, like Settings.dashboard_url or module.Settings.dashboard_url. A literal or a computed value such as Settings.dashboard_url + "/callback" raises TypeError.
  • Delegate finds the target by reading the caller's bytecode, so it runs on CPython only.

items.title: Purpose
items.text:
Demonstrates enum support:

  • StrEnum, IntEnum, IntFlag, usage via dedicated data types
  • Optional enum values
  • Bitwise flag composition (Permission)
  • Self-documenting config files with inline comments showing all allowed enum values

items.title: Running
items.text: uv run python examples/enums.py

items.title: Generated config.ini (Excerpt)
items.text:
[ServerConfig]
log_level = info  # allowed: debug, info, warning, error
default_priority = 5  # allowed: LOW(0), MEDIUM(5), HIGH(10)
default_permission = 1  # allowed: READ(1), WRITE(2), EXECUTE(4)
fallback_level = error  # allowed: debug, info, warning, error
environment = INFO  # allowed: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR

Notice how each enum value now includes an inline comment listing all possible values. This makes configuration files self-documenting for end-users who may not be familiar with the codebase.

If values are changed in code (or by assignment at runtime) they persist accordingly, and the allowed values comment is automatically maintained.

items.title: Notes
items.text:
• Allowed values are automatically displayed: Enum values include inline comments showing all valid options
  • Format varies by enum type:
  • StrEnum: Shows member values (e.g., debug, info, warning, error)
  • IntEnum/IntFlag: Shows member names with values (e.g., LOW(0), MEDIUM(5), HIGH(10))
  • Enum: Shows member names (e.g., DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR)
  • IntFlag values are stored as their integer bitfield representation
  • Optional enum fields removed (set to None) disappear from the file
  • Comments are automatically stripped when reading values, so they don't interfere with parsing

items.title: Try Variations
items.text:
• Manually set default_permission = 7 (READ|WRITE|EXECUTE) and re-run - the allowed values comment will be preserved.
  • Set fallback_level = (blank) then inspect its loaded value (None).

items.title: Purpose
items.text:
Shows how to work with list-based configuration values:

  • Storing homogeneous lists of primitives
  • Escaping separators & special characters
  • Empty elements and explicit typed empty lists

items.title: Running

items.title: Generated config.ini (Excerpt)

[ListConfig]
string_list = red,green,blue
int_list = 1,2,3,4,5

items.title: Notes
items.text:
• See List.separator and List.escape_char for their default values (explicitly set in the example for clarity).
  • Items containing the separator are escaped when written, then unescaped on read.
  • An explicit empty list with a declared data type stays as a blank line after the equals sign.

items.title: Try Variations
items.text:
• Append a value manually to int_list in the file and re-run.
  • Add a value containing a backslash and observe escaping.

items.title: Purpose
items.text:
Demonstrates nullable / optional configuration patterns:

  • optional=True shorthand vs Optional(...) wrapper
  • Optional enums, strings, integers
  • Empty string vs None semantics
  • Cascading defaults & fallback logic

items.title: Running
items.text: uv run python examples/optional_values.py

items.title: Generated config.ini (Excerpt)
items.text:
First run (only defaults materialize):

[OptionalConfig]
database_url = sqlite:///app.db
log_file = app.log
worker_count = 4
optional_string = default
optional_int = 42
optional_enum = dev
api_key = 
secret_key = 

[DatabaseConfig]
connection_string = sqlite:///fallback.db
username = 
password = 
port = 5432

After code mutates values or sets some to None, lines representing None are removed (or may remain absent if never set). When assigning new values, those lines reappear.

Example after updates:

[OptionalConfig]
database_url = 
log_file = 
worker_count = 
optional_string = new value
optional_int = 100
optional_enum = prod
api_key = 
secret_key = 

[DatabaseConfig]

username = admin
password = 
port = 5433

items.title: Notes
items.text:
• Setting a value to None for an optional field removes it from the config file.
  • Empty string "" is distinct from None (still persisted as a blank value).
  • Use fallback logic in application code (see get_connection_params).

items.title: Class vs Instance Access
items.text:
Reading configuration values works the same whether you access a Config descriptor from the class or from an instance, but setting behaves differently and is important to understand:

  • Reading: You may read values using either the class or an instance.
  • Example: AppConfig.debug and AppConfig().debug will both return the current value.
  • Setting: To write a value back through the Config descriptor you must assign on an instance.
  • Example: cfg = AppConfig(); cfg.debug = True will persist the descriptor.
  • Assigning to AppConfig.debug = True (class-level assignment) does not go through the instance write-path and therefore will not behave like an instance write, overriding the entire descriptor.

If you need class-level assignment semantics (so that AppConfig.debug = True updates configuration), use the provided metaclass ConfigContainerMeta. This metaclass adjusts container behavior so class access can be used for setting values. See tests/test_metaclass.py for a concrete example of using ConfigContainerMeta in the test-suite.

items.title: Enum Converters
items.text:
• Enum
  • StrEnum
  • IntEnum
  • IntFlag

All enum types automatically display allowed values as inline comments in the config file, making them self-documenting for end-users. For example:

log_level = info  # allowed: debug, info, warning, error

The format varies by enum type: - StrEnum: Shows member values (e.g., debug, info, warning, error) - IntEnum/IntFlag: Shows member names with integer values (e.g., LOW(0), MEDIUM(5), HIGH(10)) - Enum: Shows member names (e.g., DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR)

Comments are automatically stripped when reading values, ensuring they don't interfere with parsing.

items.title: Multiple Instances Behavior
items.text:
• Test reference: tests/test_two_instances.py — verifies that two instances of the same Config-container class observe the same values and that the descriptor-level on_file_change handler is invoked when the backing file is updated.
  • Singleton-like behavior: When multiple instances are created from the same config-container class, they share the underlying parser and descriptor state. Mutating a value through one instance (or via the descriptor) is observable from the other instance; this is effectively a shared/singleton configuration surface backed by a single parser.
  • Descriptor-level hooks: on_file_change is attached to the descriptor (not per-instance) in the test. This means file-change callbacks are shared across instances of the same config class and will fire when the FileWatcher indicates the file has changed.
  • Practical implication: Treat config-container classes as views over a shared configuration store. Writes performed on any instance or via the descriptor update the shared parser and (when enabled) persist to the configured file.
